clue.text: Grandtutorial Ideal Laboratory Eugenical Specimen father of George

definitions.meaning: in John Barth's novel ... Goat-Boy the hero's title is an acronym formed from these words
the Grand-Tutorial specimen is the hero George's begetter in Barth's campus allegory

explanation.surface: A mock-academic title strung out before a reference to a family of the Georges.
explanation.definitionFit: Barth's novel Giles Goat-Boy builds its hero's name from the initials of that pseudo-scientific title.

clue.text: Views do go in different directions for such Alcottian paragons (4, )

indicators.note: the letters of these three words are scattered and set off afresh in a new order

explanation.surface: Opinions diverge over the virtuous women of Louisa May Alcott's fiction.
explanation.definitionFit: Good Wives is the sequel to Little Women by Louisa May Alcott, its title naming model housewives.

clue.text: French novelist keeps time for Venetian composer

indicators.note: a novelist who keeps something holds it within himself, so one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: Pierre Loti was a French naval officer and novelist

explanation.surface: A French writer holds on to a period, leading us to a composer from Venice.
explanation.definitionFit: Antonio Lotti was a Baroque composer and organist at St Mark's in Venice.

clue.text: Heinlein's cavalrymen accompanied this sort of enterprise

definitions.meaning: Robert Heinlein's novel names its mobile infantry troopers after a spacecraft
the Star Trek Enterprise is a vessel of this kind

explanation.surface: Heinlein's mounted soldiers went along on a bold venture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'enterprise' reads as a business venture but points to the Star Trek ship Enterprise; Heinlein's novel is Starship Troopers.
explanation.definitionFit: A spacecraft for interstellar travel, as in Heinlein's Troopers and Star Trek's Enterprise.

clue.text: She was finally shepherded home, after the fall of Troy

definitions.text: She was finally shepherded home, after the fall of Troy

parts.words: She was finally shepherded home, after the fall of Troy
parts.note: in Hardy's Far from the Madding Crowd the heroine marries the shepherd Gabriel Oak after Sergeant Troy is killed

explanation.surface: A woman of ancient legend returns home once the city of Troy has fallen.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests Helen and the Trojan War; Troy is Hardy's Sergeant Troy, and the shepherd is Gabriel Oak.
explanation.definitionFit: Bathsheba Everdene, Hardy's heroine, finally weds the faithful shepherd once her husband Troy is dead.

clue.text: Lovers of Spillane

parts.note: Mickey Spillane wrote a Mike Hammer thriller whose title completes this phrase with a word for a corpse

explanation.surface: Fans of the hard-boiled crime writer Mickey Spillane.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lovers of Spillane' looks like his readers; it is the title The Body Lovers with its first word missing.
explanation.definitionFit: The Body Lovers (1967) is a Mike Hammer novel by Mickey Spillane, so the missing word is the corpse.

clue.text: One third of cat's portion each from Stein, Auchinloss and Lettice Cooper (5, )

definitions.meaning: a cat is said to have nine lives, and a third of that allowance is the number asked for

definitions.text: each from Stein, Auchinloss and Lettice Cooper
definitions.meaning: Gertrude Stein, Louis Auchincloss and Lettice Cooper each published a book with this title

explanation.surface: A fraction of a cat's allotment is shared out among three writers.
explanation.definitionFit: Nine lives divided by three gives the number, and Stein's 1909 book of novellas bears the same title.

clue.text: Iroquois stoic?

definitions.meaning: one of the six nations of the Iroquois confederacy in what is now New York State
the Roman philosopher and dramatist who taught Stoicism to Nero

explanation.surface: Is a member of an Iroquois people impassive by nature?
explanation.definitionFit: The Seneca are an Iroquois nation, and Lucius Annaeus Seneca was the Roman Stoic philosopher.

clue.text: Weapon of former bore, they say

indicators.note: what people say is heard rather than written, so the spoken form of the phrase is wanted

parts.note: EX means former and CALIBRE is the bore of a gun barrel

explanation.surface: A weapon that used to be dull, so people claim.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bore' looks like a tedious person but is a gun's calibre.
explanation.definitionFit: King Arthur's sword is the most famous named weapon in legend.

clue.text: An extremely good children's writer

parts.note: extremely and very are both intensifiers meaning to a high degree

explanation.surface: Praise for a fine author of books for the young.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue reads naturally as 'a very good children's writer', which is how it describes Gillian Avery.
explanation.definitionFit: Gillian Avery was a noted English author and historian of children's books.

clue.text: Rule provides eponymous alien

definitions.meaning: the Canadian novelist Jane Rule wrote a book of this name
a foreigner or stranger who gives a book its title

explanation.surface: A regulation supplies the title character, a stranger from elsewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rule' looks like a law but is the novelist Jane Rule.
explanation.definitionFit: An outsider or foreigner, and the title of Jane Rule's 1981 collection.

clue.text: Suitable place for some sculpture in scenic Hertfordshire

indicators.note: the letters sit inside the run of these two words, spanning the gap between them

explanation.surface: A good spot for a statue in a picturesque home county.
explanation.definitionFit: A recess in a wall built to display a statue or ornament.

clue.text: Fancy sounding like a renowned detective!

indicators.note: the word is chosen because it is spoken the same as the name

parts.note: Lord Peter Wimsey is Dorothy L. Sayers's aristocratic sleuth

explanation.surface: A notion that recalls a famous fictional investigator.
explanation.definitionFit: Playful fancy or caprice, a light flight of imagination.

clue.text: Magically significant line on seat describing Algonquin humorist

indicators.note: in an across clue one piece written on another follows it

parts.note: a bench is a long seat
a ley line is an alignment of ancient sites credited with mystical power

explanation.surface: A mystical alignment runs across a seat that portrays a wit of the Algonquin Round Table.
explanation.walkthrough: The Algonquin Round Table was a circle of New York wits; Robert Benchley was one.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Benchley was an American humorist and a founder of the Algonquin Round Table.

clue.text: Smart rogues and rascals take something for granted?

definitions.text: Smart rogues and rascals take something for granted?

parts.words: Smart rogues and rascals take something for granted?
parts.note: the clue describes cheeky villains appropriating things, while the question mark hints at a premise accepted without proof

explanation.surface: Clever scoundrels help themselves to things as if by right.
explanation.definitionFit: Something taken for granted is a premise or presupposition accepted without proof.

clue.text: Turgenev offered maids fuel?

parts.note: maids in the old sense are unmarried young women, virgins
oil is a fuel

explanation.surface: Did the Russian novelist offer housemaids something to burn?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turgenev offered' stands for a book he gave the world: his novel Virgin Soil (1877).
explanation.definitionFit: Virgin Soil is Ivan Turgenev's last novel, about Russian populists.

clue.text: Rest of unreadable book?

definitions.meaning: what is left over
an unsold book cleared at a reduced price, as though nobody would read it

explanation.surface: Is the rest of it a book nobody can read?
explanation.definitionFit: The leftover part, and publishers' unsold stock sold off cheaply.

clue.text: It follows former pupil in potted biography

indicators.note: one piece comes after the other in the answer

parts.note: OB is old boy, a former pupil of a school

explanation.surface: Something comes after an old boy in a short life story.
explanation.definitionFit: A short obituary notice is a compressed life story.

clue.text: "Let old yield the prize " (Dryden, Alexander's Feast)

definitions.text: "Let old yield the prize " (Dryden, Alexander's Feast)

parts.words: "Let old yield the prize " (Dryden, Alexander's Feast)
parts.note: the missing name in Dryden's line is the musician of Alexander the Great, outdone by Saint Cecilia

explanation.surface: A line from Dryden's ode with a name left out.
explanation.definitionFit: Dryden's ode closes 'Let old Timotheus yield the prize, Or both divide the crown', naming Alexander's court musician.

clue.text: Apart from Terence's tables

definitions.meaning: kept away from one another
Terence Rattigan wrote the play ... Tables, set in a seaside hotel

explanation.surface: Away from the tables of the Roman comic poet Terence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Terence' suggests the Roman dramatist; it is Terence Rattigan.
explanation.definitionFit: Not joined together, and the adjective in Rattigan's play title Separate Tables.

clue.text: I am in the vessel with one who knew how the poor live

definitions.text: one who knew how the poor live

indicators.note: one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: SS is steamship, a vessel
I'm is the short form of I am

explanation.surface: I am aboard ship alongside someone who knew poverty.
explanation.definitionFit: George R. Sims wrote How the Poor Live (1883), a study of London slums.

clue.text: Mere Augean clean-up from Bulwer Lytton's dominie

indicators.note: tidying the letters puts them into a new order, as in cleaning the Augean stables

explanation.surface: A mere Augean cleansing taken from a Bulwer-Lytton schoolmaster.
explanation.walkthrough: A dominie is a schoolmaster; Eugene Aram was a real murderer-schoolmaster fictionalised by Bulwer-Lytton.
explanation.definitionFit: Bulwer-Lytton's novel Eugene Aram tells of a scholarly schoolmaster who was a murderer.

clue.text: White Italian female might support the house in Heman's verse

definitions.meaning: the Italian word for white in its feminine form, and a girl's name

definitions.text: might support the house in Heman's verse
definitions.meaning: a heroine of Felicia Hemans's verse bears this Italian name

explanation.surface: A fair Italian woman might prop up the household in a Hemans poem.
explanation.definitionFit: Italian for white in the feminine, also a woman's name used by the poet Felicia Hemans.

clue.text: Macedonian king gets Greek letter in battle

parts.note: Philip II of Macedon, father of Alexander the Great
pi is a letter of the Greek alphabet

explanation.surface: A king of Macedon acquires a Greek letter during a battle.
explanation.definitionFit: Antony and Octavian defeated Brutus and Cassius at Philippi in 42 BC.

clue.text: Quiet put-down of habit in Scott ()

parts.note: P is piano, the musical direction for quiet
laid means put down

explanation.surface: A quiet snub about a nun's habit in Walter Scott.
explanation.walkthrough: 'habit' means clothing, the tartan cloak of Scott's Highland novels.
explanation.definitionFit: A plaid is a tartan wrap worn as Highland dress, as described in Scott's novels.

clue.text: When I'm alone with Barker, for instance I'm as chatty as (P. G. Wodehouse, Jill the Reckless)

definitions.text: When I'm alone with Barker, for instance I'm as chatty as (P. G. Wodehouse, Jill the Reckless)

parts.words: When I'm alone with Barker, for instance I'm as chatty as (P. G. Wodehouse, Jill the Reckless)
parts.note: a quotation from Wodehouse with the closing word left out, to be supplied from the novel

explanation.surface: A Wodehouse line about talking freely with Barker, its last word missing.
explanation.definitionFit: The word completing the Wodehouse quotation from Jill the Reckless, an exclamation used as a comic comparison.

clue.text: He wears the crown, like Shaw's heroine

definitions.meaning: an army officer of this rank wears a crown on his shoulder
... Barbara is the Salvation Army heroine of Shaw's play

explanation.surface: A monarch is compared to a heroine of George Bernard Shaw.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wears the crown' suggests a king; in the British Army the insignia of this rank is a crown.
explanation.definitionFit: A British Army officer's rank badge is a crown, and Barbara Undershaft holds that rank in Shaw's play.

clue.text: Identification with measure of Jefferies's father in fiction

parts.note: ID is the short form of identification; the first letters being the same is a coincidence
an en is a printer's measure of width

explanation.surface: Paperwork plus a measurement for a fictional father by Richard Jefferies.
explanation.definitionFit: In Richard Jefferies's novel Bevis, the boy's father is Farmer Iden.

clue.text: Gold study for poet

parts.note: Au is the chemical symbol for gold
a den is a private study

explanation.surface: Precious metal and a room for working, all for a poet.
explanation.definitionFit: W. H. Auden was an Anglo-American poet.

clue.text: Tom Sawyer's brave personification of evil

definitions.meaning: the half-Native American villain of Mark Twain's novel, a brave being a Native American warrior
the murderer who embodies wickedness in the story of Tom and Huck

explanation.surface: The courageous embodiment of wickedness in Mark Twain's novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brave' reads as courageous but is a Native American warrior.
explanation.definitionFit: Injun Joe is the murderous villain of Mark Twain's The Adventures of Tom Sawyer.

clue.text: An adept with cloak, dagger, sword and musket

definitions.text: An adept with cloak, dagger, sword and musket

parts.words: An adept with cloak, dagger, sword and musket
parts.note: describes Dumas's swashbuckling Gascon who joins the King's Musketeers

explanation.surface: Someone expert in espionage and swordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Dumas's Gascon hero joins the Musketeers and excels at swordplay and intrigue.

clue.text: Nobility of Lear's wordplay

indicators.note: playing with the word means its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: The nobles in King Lear and the play on words.
explanation.definitionFit: Peers of the realm, members of the aristocracy.
